{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-01",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["Password reset request form", "Reset token generator", "Email delivery", "Public reset page", "Session issuance", "Login page"],
    "dataStores": ["User credential store", "Reset token store"],
    "externalServices": ["Email provider"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Internet to public reset page", "Application to email delivery channel"],
    "dataClasses": ["pii", "credentials"],
    "exposure": "public",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Clicking the reset link logs the visitor in, so anyone holding the link owns the account",
      "scenario": "The reset link doubles as an authenticated session. Anyone who gets the URL (shared mailbox, forwarded mail, mail-scanning gateway, browser history on a shared PC, referrer leak to third-party assets on the public reset page) can open it and is logged in immediately, without knowing the old password or any second factor. Full account takeover of an internet-facing account with PII.",
      "component": "Public reset page / session issuance",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Clicking it opens a public page where the user sets a new password and is logged in immediately." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V6.3.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-640"],
      "plainLanguage": "The emailed link is as good as the password: whoever opens it is signed in as that user.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Do not grant a session from the reset link alone",
        "given": "a user opens a valid password reset link",
        "when": "the new password is submitted successfully",
        "then": "the reset token is consumed and the user is redirected to the normal login flow (including any second factor) instead of being issued an authenticated session directly from the link"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Reset token stays usable for 24 hours, giving attackers a long window",
      "scenario": "A 24-hour validity window gives an attacker who gains temporary mailbox access, intercepts a mail relay, or finds the link in logs or history a full day to use it. It also means an unused link from a reset the victim never asked for remains live long after the victim ignored the email.",
      "component": "Reset token generator",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The link contains a token valid for 24 hours." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V6.3.4"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-613"],
      "plainLanguage": "A reset link that works all day gives an attacker plenty of time to find and use it.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Short-lived, high-entropy, single-use reset token",
        "given": "a password reset is requested",
        "when": "the token is generated",
        "then": "it is at least 128 bits of cryptographically random data, expires within 15 minutes, is stored only as a hash, and is invalidated on first successful use"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Old sessions and outstanding reset links are not invalidated after a password change",
      "scenario": "The design says nothing about terminating other sessions or revoking other tokens. An attacker who already hijacked a session, or who requested an extra reset link, keeps access after the victim resets their password, so the victim's recovery does not evict the intruder and the attacker can reset the password again later.",
      "component": "Session issuance / reset token store",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Clicking it opens a public page where the user sets a new password and is logged in immediately." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V7.4.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-613"],
      "plainLanguage": "After a reset, an intruder's existing login and spare reset links should stop working, but nothing says they do.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Revoke sessions and tokens on password change",
        "given": "a user completes a password reset",
        "when": "the new password is stored",
        "then": "all other active sessions, remember-me tokens and outstanding reset tokens for that account are invalidated and the user is notified by email"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Reset request form reveals which email addresses have accounts",
      "scenario": "An attacker submits candidate email addresses to the internet-facing reset form. If the response, timing or wording differs for registered and unregistered addresses, the attacker builds a confirmed list of users of the service, which is PII in itself and feeds credential stuffing and phishing against those users.",
      "component": "Password reset request form",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Users who forget their password request a reset link by email address." },
        { "quote": "The login page is internet-facing." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-204"],
      "plainLanguage": "Typing an email into the forgot-password form should not tell a stranger whether that person has an account.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Uniform response to reset requests",
        "given": "an anonymous user submits any email address to the reset form",
        "when": "the account does or does not exist",
        "then": "the same message, status code and response timing are returned, and mail is sent only to existing accounts"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Unauthenticated reset endpoint can be abused to flood a victim's inbox or the mail quota",
      "scenario": "The reset form is public and requires no authentication. An attacker scripts thousands of requests for one victim address to bury real mail and pressure the victim into clicking a link, or for many addresses to exhaust the email provider's sending quota and reputation, blocking resets for all legitimate users.",
      "component": "Password reset request form / email delivery",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Users who forget their password request a reset link by email address." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-770"],
      "plainLanguage": "Anyone can hit the forgot-password button in a loop and spam a user's inbox or use up the email budget.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Throttle reset requests per address and per source",
        "given": "reset requests arrive for the same email address or from the same source",
        "when": "a configured threshold is exceeded in a time window",
        "then": "further requests are rejected without sending mail, existing unexpired links are reused rather than regenerated, and the event is alerted on"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Reset link in email is the only identity check, with no second factor or notification",
      "scenario": "Possession of one email message fully replaces the account password. An attacker who has phished or compromised the victim's mailbox, or who controls a recycled/aliased address, takes over the application account silently because no second factor is requested and the design mentions no confirmation to the user that a reset happened.",
      "component": "Reset flow trust boundary",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Users who forget their password request a reset link by email address." },
        { "quote": "Clicking it opens a public page where the user sets a new password and is logged in immediately." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V6.3.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-620"],
      "plainLanguage": "Whoever controls the mailbox controls the account, and the real user is never told it happened.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Second factor and change notification on recovery",
        "given": "an account has a second factor enrolled",
        "when": "a password reset link is used",
        "then": "the second factor is required before the password can be changed, and a notification email is sent to the account address for every completed reset"
      }
    }
  ]
}
